# Textual data {#sec-text}

::: {.content-hidden}
PLAN (Oct 2026)

Keep the book's probabilistic framing throughout: anomalous documents have high surprisal under a language model, or low density in a feature space; authorship verification is a one-class problem (is this text surprising given the author's known work?).

1. From text to numbers (brief)
   - Tokens, document-term matrix, tf-idf, function vs content words, using tidytext (Silge & Robinson, Text Mining with R).

2. Bag-of-words anomalies
   - Document features: length, type-token ratio, word and sentence length, punctuation, sentiment, readability, out-of-vocabulary share.
     Then HDR / stray / LOF on the feature matrix (parallels the ch13 features strategy).
   - Example: wine review descriptions.
     Needs the original `description` column (dropped by fetch_wine_reviews()) restored in the weird package, giving one data set with numerical, categorical and text variables.
     Natural target: reviews whose wording disagrees with their points.

3. Language-model surprisals
   - Unigram / n-gram models give each document a surprisal; perplexity = exp(mean surprisal).
     Show which words drive a document's score.
   - Topic models (LDA) for unusual topic mixtures; document embeddings + PCA (link to ch9).
   - Example: wine review descriptions (same data as section 2).
   - Discussion: detectors of machine-generated text (DetectGPT, Binoculars) flag text that is too predictable, i.e. unusually LOW surprisal.

4. Was this text written by someone else?
   - Authorship verification as one-class anomaly detection; function-word rates per chunk; Burrows' Delta mentioned as the stylometric standard (Manhattan distance on z-scores, ignores correlations).
   - Example: The Royal Book of Oz (1921), credited to L Frank Baum but written by Ruth Plumly Thompson (Binongo, 2003, Chance); fetch_oz_books() (14 Baum, 15 Thompson).
   - Model of Baum's style: Normal distribution fitted to Baum's chunks (clean subset, as in BACON); surprisals = Mahalanobis (ch6); leave-one-book-out surprisals as the reference sample; rank approximation; book surprisal = sum of chunk surprisals (as tokens in section 3).
   - Where the differences hide: Thompson's chunks differ along Baum's smallest-variance principal components (hidden anomalies, ch3); outlier map shows residual-space anomalies (ch9); explains why Delta and a 2-D projection do less well.

Data for the weird package (book must not download from Gutenberg at build time; gutenbergr only in data-raw):

- `description` column restored in wine_reviews
- fetch_oz_books(): paragraphs of 29 Oz books (Baum 14, Thompson 15)

New book dependencies: tidytext.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup11
#| include: false
#| cache: false

source("before-each-chapter.R")
```

Text is an extreme example of categorical data (@sec-categorical-data).
Each word comes from a vocabulary of many thousands of words, most of which are rarely used, and a document is a sequence of words whose meaning depends on their order.
A document is anomalous if it is improbable under a model of the language in which it is written, or if it has features that are very different from other documents in a given corpus.

The chapter starts by converting documents to numbers, and then finds anomalous documents from their features or from their surprisals under a language model.
Then it explores whether a document is surprising given other documents thought to be from the same author; this can help in identifying misattributed authorship.

The first two approaches are illustrated using the tasters' descriptions in the wine reviews data, so that the anomalous descriptions can be compared with the other variables recorded for each wine.
The authorship example uses the Oz books of L. Frank Baum and Ruth Plumly Thompson, including one published under Baum's name after his death.
A fuller introduction to analysing text in R is given by @Silge2017.

## From text to numbers {#sec-text-numbers}

Documents cannot be analysed using the methods of @sec-categorical-data, because each contains many words (categorical values), and almost every document is unique.
One relatively simple approach to analysing textual data is to convert each document to a vector of numbers by counting how often each word occurs in it, treating it as a **bag of words** and ignoring the order of the words.
While this loses much of the meaning of the text, it is enough to find many kinds of anomalous documents.

The examples in this section and the next use the tasters' descriptions of the `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` wines in the wine reviews data (@sec-data).
They form a large collection of short documents, each describing a wine.
Here are three of them.

```{r}
#| label: fetch-wine-reviews-text
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

wine_reviews <- fetch_wine_reviews()
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-descriptions
#| code-fold: false
#| class-output: wrap

wine_reviews |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(description)
```

Our task is to find reviews that are substantially different from the other reviews in the data set.

### Tokens and vocabulary

A **token** is a unit of text, and splitting a document into tokens is called **tokenisation**.
Depending on the analysis, the tokens might be single characters, words, pairs of adjacent words, or whole sentences, but in this chapter every token is a single word.
The `unnest_tokens()` function from the **`tidytext`** package\ [@Silge2017] splits text into words by default.
It converts the text to lower case, removes the punctuation, and returns one row for each token, here in a column called `word`.
To keep track of which document each token came from, an `id` column, giving the row number of each review, is added to the data first.

```{r}
#| label: tidytext
#| code-fold: false
#| cache: false

library(tidytext)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-descriptions

wine_reviews <- wine_reviews |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)
wine_words <- wine_reviews |>
  select(id, variety, description) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, description, token = "words")
wine_words
vocabulary <- wine_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)
vocabulary
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-words-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-words

top10_share <- sum(vocabulary$n[1:10]) / sum(vocabulary$n)
once_share <- mean(vocabulary$n == 1)
stop_share <- mean(wine_words$word %in% stop_words$word)
# The prose describes the size of the vocabulary and the most common words
stopifnot(
  NROW(wine_words) > 4.5e6,
  between(NROW(vocabulary), 32000, 33000),
  round(100 * once_share) == 38,
  round(100 * top10_share) == 27,
  all(vocabulary$word[1:7] == c("and", "the", "a", "of", "with", "this", "is")),
  vocabulary$word[8] == "wine",
  NROW(stop_words) == 1149,
  round(100 * stop_share) == 44
)
```

The `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` descriptions contain `r sprintf("%.1f", NROW(wine_words) / 1e6)` million tokens, but only `r scales::comma(NROW(vocabulary))` distinct words, which together form the **vocabulary**.
A few words are used very often: the ten most common words account for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * top10_share)`% of the tokens.
At the other extreme, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * once_share)`% of the vocabulary occurs only once.
This follows the pattern found in almost every large collection of text, known as **Zipf's law**\ [@Zipf1949]: the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in the list of word frequencies.

Each token is therefore an observation of a categorical variable whose categories are the words of the vocabulary: tens of thousands of categories, most of them rare.
The probability of each word can be estimated from its frequency, as in @sec-categorical, but for most words this estimate rests on only a handful of occurrences, and many possible words don't occur at all.

### Function words and content words

The most common words are "and", "the", "a", "of", "with", "this" and "is".
These are **function words**, which give a sentence its grammatical structure, as distinct from **content words**, such as "wine", "cherry" and "tannins", which carry its meaning.
Lists of function words and other very common words are called **stop words**.

The `stop_words` data in **`tidytext`** combine three overlapping lists, giving `r scales::comma(n_distinct(stop_words$word))` distinct words that account for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * stop_share)`% of the tokens in the descriptions.
Stop words are usually removed when the aim is to find what a document is about, but they are useful words for describing *how* it is written.
Patterns in how a writer uses these little words can help to identify the writer.

Removing them with `anti_join()` leaves the content words.

```{r}
#| label: wine-content-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

vocabulary |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")
```

### The document-term matrix

The word counts of a collection of $n$ documents form an $n \times m$ **document-term matrix**, with one row for each document and one column for each of the $m$ words in the vocabulary.
The entry in row $i$ and column $w$ is $t_{iw}$, the number of times word $w$ occurs in document $i$.
The sums of each row and column, and the numbers of non-zero entries in each row and column, provide simple summaries of the documents and the words:

- $t_{i \cdot} = \sum_w t_{iw}$, the sum of row $i$, is the number of tokens in document $i$;
- $t_{\cdot w} = \sum_i t_{iw}$, the sum of column $w$, is the number of times word $w$ occurs in the whole collection, which is the frequency used to rank the vocabulary above;
- $m_i$, the number of non-zero entries in row $i$, is the number of distinct words in document $i$, so $m_i \le t_{i \cdot}$ and $m_i \le m$;
- $n_w$, the number of non-zero entries in column $w$, is the number of documents that contain word $w$, called its **document frequency**, so $n_w \le n$.

The total of all the entries, $\sum_i t_{i \cdot} = \sum_w t_{\cdot w}$, is the number of tokens in the collection.
The `cast_sparse()` function builds the matrix from the word counts.

```{r}
#| label: wine-dtm
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

dtm <- wine_words |>
  count(id, word) |>
  cast_sparse(id, word, n)
dim(dtm)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-dtm-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-dtm

dtm_density <- Matrix::nnzero(dtm) / prod(dim(dtm))
stopifnot(
  NROW(dtm) == NROW(wine_reviews),
  NCOL(dtm) == NROW(vocabulary),
  round(100 * dtm_density, 1) == 0.1
)
```

Each description is now a point in a space with $m =$ `r scales::comma(NCOL(dtm))` dimensions, but only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dtm_density)`% of the entries are non-zero, so the matrix is stored in a sparse form.
The methods of @sec-highdim could in principle be applied to its rows, but most of the columns are almost entirely zero, and the counts of common words such as "the" contribute far more to any distance between rows than those of rarer words.
So the counts are usually reweighted, or reduced to a few features.

### Term frequency--inverse document frequency

The **term frequency** of word $w$ in document $i$ is the proportion of the document's tokens that are that word, $\text{tf}_{iw} = t_{iw}/t_{i \cdot}$.
The **inverse document frequency** of word $w$ depends on its document frequency $n_w$:
$$
  \text{idf}_w = \log(n / n_w),
$$
which is zero for a word that occurs in every document, and largest for a word that occurs in only one\ [@SparckJones1972].
The product $\text{tf}_{iw} \times \text{idf}_w$, called **tf-idf**, is large for words that are common in document $i$ but rare in the other documents, so it picks out the words that distinguish a document from the rest.
Replacing the counts in the document-term matrix by their tf-idf values gives rare words more weight than common ones, much as MCA gives rare categories more weight (@sec-correspondence).

@fig-wine-tfidf shows the words that are most characteristic of six grape varieties, found by treating all the descriptions of each variety as a single document and computing the tf-idf of each word with `bind_tf_idf()`, using all the varieties in the data as the collection of documents.
The words in the names of the varieties (such as "pinot" and "noir") are removed first, as they are trivially characteristic.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-tfidf
#| dependson: wine-words
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   The six words with the largest tf-idf in the descriptions of each of six grape varieties, treating all the descriptions of each variety as a single document.
#| fig-height: 4.5

variety_words <- wine_reviews |>
  distinct(variety) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, variety)
variety_tfidf <- wine_words |>
  filter(!is.na(variety)) |>
  anti_join(variety_words, by = "word") |>
  count(variety, word) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, variety, n)
varieties <- c(
  "Chardonnay",
  "Pinot Noir",
  "Riesling",
  "Sauvignon Blanc",
  "Syrah",
  "Zinfandel"
)
variety_tfidf |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 6, by = variety, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, variety))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(variety), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(x = "tf-idf", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-tfidf-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: fig-wine-tfidf

top_tfidf <- variety_tfidf |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 6, by = variety, with_ties = FALSE)
has <- function(v, w) all(w %in% top_tfidf$word[top_tfidf$variety == v])
sweetness <- wine_reviews |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  summarise(
    dry = mean(grepl("\\b(dry|sweet)\\b", description, ignore.case = TRUE)),
    .by = variety
  )
# The prose describes the words in fig-wine-tfidf
stopifnot(
  has("Chardonnay", c("oak", "buttered", "pineapple", "toast")),
  has("Pinot Noir", c("cola", "raspberry", "cranberry")),
  has("Riesling", c("lime", "peach", "tangerine", "dry", "off")),
  has("Sauvignon Blanc", c("gooseberry", "grapefruit", "sb")),
  has("Syrah", c("pepper", "meat")),
  has("Zinfandel", c("alcohol", "zin")),
  sweetness$variety[which.max(sweetness$dry)] == "Riesling"
)
```

Most of the words are what a wine drinker would expect: the oak, buttered toast and pineapple of Chardonnay, the cola, raspberry and cranberry of Pinot Noir, the lime, peach and tangerine of Riesling, the gooseberry and grapefruit of Sauvignon Blanc, the pepper and meat of Syrah, and the alcohol of Zinfandel.
The words "dry" and "off" (as in "off-dry") appear for Riesling, whose reviews often say how sweet the wine is.
The tasters' abbreviations "zin" and "sb" survive the removal of the variety names.

## Bag-of-words anomalies {#sec-text-bow}

Although a bag of words ignores the order of the words, the word counts can still reveal anomalous documents in two ways.
First, each document can be summarised by a few interpretable features, such as its length or its tone, and the multivariate methods of earlier chapters applied to find documents with unusual features.
Second, the other variables recorded with each document can be modelled conditionally on its word counts, to find documents whose words disagree with those variables.

### Reviews with unusual features

The features used here measure the length of a document, its style, its vocabulary and its tone:

- `words`: the number of words;
- `word_length`: the mean number of characters in each word;
- `function_words`: the proportion of the words that are stop words;
- `idf`: the mean of the inverse document frequencies of the words, which is large when a document uses words that are rare in the collection;
- `sentiment`: the number of positive words minus the number of negative words, divided by the number of words, using the list of `r scales::comma(n_distinct(get_sentiments()$word))` positive and negative words compiled by @Hu2004;
- `punctuation`: the number of punctuation marks for each word.

Apart from `punctuation`, the features are computed from the word counts of a document: `words` is their total, and the others are averages over the words of the document, weighted by their counts.
All but `idf` depend only on the document itself; `idf` also depends on the whole collection, through the number of documents containing each word.

Each of the `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` descriptions is treated as a document, and the six features are computed for each one.
Because the documents are now descriptions rather than varieties, $n_w$ in `idf` is the number of descriptions containing word $w$, not the number of varieties as in @fig-wine-tfidf.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-features
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

idf <- wine_words |>
  distinct(id, word) |>
  count(word) |>
  mutate(idf = log(NROW(wine_reviews) / n)) |>
  select(word, idf)
text_features <- wine_words |>
  left_join(idf, by = "word") |>
  left_join(get_sentiments() |> filter(n() == 1, .by = word), by = "word") |>
  summarise(
    words = n(),
    word_length = mean(nchar(word)),
    function_words = mean(word %in% stop_words$word),
    idf = mean(idf),
    sentiment = (sum(sentiment == "positive", na.rm = TRUE) -
      sum(sentiment == "negative", na.rm = TRUE)) /
      n(),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  left_join(
    wine_reviews |> select(id, points, description),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    punctuation = stringr::str_count(description, "[[:punct:]]") / words,
    .after = sentiment
  )
text_features
```

The reviews are relatively short, with a median of `r median(text_features$words)` words, so the features will be noisy, especially for the shortest reviews.

The number of words is replaced by its logarithm, the features are converted to robust multivariate $z$-scores with `mvscale()` (@sec-scaling), and a Gaussian mixture model (@sec-gmm-surprisal) is fitted to the scaled features.
Its surprisal probabilities are computed using the GPD approximation of @sec-approximate-surprisal-prob, as the mixture model is unlikely to fit the tails of the distribution well.
With more than 100,000 reviews, fitting the mixture takes several minutes.

```{r}
#| label: mclust-text
#| message: false
#| code-fold: false
#| cache: false

library(mclust)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

Z <- text_features |>
  mutate(words = log(words)) |>
  select(words:punctuation) |>
  mvscale() |>
  as.matrix()
set.seed(1967)
text_gmm <- Mclust(Z, verbose = FALSE) |>
  dist_mclust()
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm-fit
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-features

Z <- text_features |>
  mutate(words = log(words)) |>
  select(words:punctuation) |>
  mvscale() |>
  as.matrix()
set.seed(1967)
text_gmm <- Mclust(Z, verbose = FALSE) |>
  dist_mclust() |>
  cache("wine_text_gmm")
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm-fit

text_features <- text_features |>
  mutate(
    s = surprisals(Z, distribution = text_gmm),
    p = surprisals_prob(Z, distribution = text_gmm, approximation = "gpd"),
    flagged = p < 0.001
  )
text_features |>
  arrange(p) |>
  select(points, words:punctuation, p, flagged)
```

The texts of the twelve least probable reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-top
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm
#| class-output: wrap

text_features |> slice_min(p, n = 12) |> pull(description)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-top

flagged_text <- text_features |> filter(flagged)
top_text <- text_features |> arrange(p) |> head(12)
non_review <- grepl("^Imported by|not available", text_features$description)
flagged_non_review <- grepl(
  "^Imported by|not available",
  flagged_text$description
)
short_reviews <- flagged_text |> filter(words <= 10, !flagged_non_review)
percentages <- grepl("%", flagged_text$description)
punct_q99 <- quantile(text_features$punctuation, 0.99)
high_punct <- flagged_text$punctuation > punct_q99
gaultier <- text_features |> filter(grepl("Gaultier", description))
# The prose describes the reviews with the smallest surprisal probabilities
stopifnot(
  NROW(get_sentiments()) == 6786,
  sum(non_review) == 7,
  all(text_features$p[non_review] < 0.001),
  sum(grepl("^Imported by|not available", top_text$description[1:7])) == 6,
  all(top_text$words[1:7] <= 7),
  grepl("^Smells raisiny", top_text$description[7]),
  all(top_text$words <= 12),
  NROW(short_reviews) >= 10,
  median(short_reviews$points) < quantile(text_features$points, 0.05),
  sum(high_punct) >= 20,
  sum(high_punct & flagged_text$words > 10) >= sum(flagged_text$words > 10) / 3,
  sum(percentages) >= 5,
  sum(percentages & high_punct) > sum(percentages) / 2,
  NROW(gaultier) == 1,
  gaultier$p < 0.001,
  between(NROW(flagged_text), 60, 110),
  sum(flagged_text$words <= 10) >= 15,
  all(flagged_text$words < 100),
  sum(flagged_text$words > 10) >= 25
)
```

`r english::Words(NROW(flagged_text))` reviews have surprisal probabilities below 0.001.
Seven of the eight least probable are not reviews at all, but say only that the wine was "Imported by" a named company, or that the review is not available.
The other reviews printed above are very terse, such as "Smells raisiny, feels hot, tastes overripe.", and dismiss the wine in a few words.
The flagged reviews with ten words or fewer have a median of `r median(short_reviews$points)` points, lower than 95% of all reviews.
Many of the longer flagged reviews have much more punctuation than usual: `r english::words(sum(high_punct))` of the flagged reviews have more punctuation marks per word than 99% of all reviews, including most of those that list the percentages of the vineyards or grape varieties in a blend.
Another flagged review is mostly about the packaging rather than the wine: a red vinyl body suit designed for the bottle by the fashion designer Jean-Paul Gaultier.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-text-features
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Number of words and mean inverse document frequency of the wine review descriptions.
#|   The reviews with surprisal probabilities below 0.001, under a Gaussian mixture model of the six text features, are shown in orange.
#| fig-height: 3.5

text_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = words, y = idf)) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(text_features, p >= 0.001),
    width = 0.01,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.05,
    size = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(text_features, p < 0.001),
    width = 0.01,
    height = 0,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of words (log scale)", y = "Mean idf")
```

@fig-wine-text-features shows two of the six features.
The descriptions that are not reviews are at the top left, with only a few words, most of them rare.
Many of the other flagged reviews are very short, and the rest are flagged because of their other features, or their combination of features.

### Reviews that disagree with their points

A review can also be anomalous because its text does not fit its other variables.
The points awarded to a wine, on a scale of 80 to 100, should agree with what the taster wrote about it, so a review whose points are surprising given its wording is a **conditional anomaly**, even if neither its points nor its wording is unusual on its own.
As in @sec-mixed, such anomalies are found from the conditional surprisal, $-\log f(\text{points} \mid \text{text})$, here estimated by a linear regression with Normal errors (@sec-regression-log-scores).

The six features above are not much use as predictors, as only the sentiment score measures whether a review is favourable, and it uses a general list of words that knows nothing about wine.
The predictors used instead are the counts of the most common words (those used in at least 500 reviews), along with the logarithm of the number of words.
Each coefficient is then the change in the expected points for each use of that word, holding the other predictors fixed.
The seven descriptions that are not reviews are removed first: an import statement, or a note that the review is not available, says nothing about the wine, so it can neither agree nor disagree with the points.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-reviews
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm

reviews <- text_features |>
  filter(!grepl("^Imported by|not available", description))
```

The regression model has more than 100,000 observations and nearly 1,000 predictors.
To save memory, `model = FALSE` stops `lm()` from storing another copy of the design matrix in its model frame.
Even so, the fitted model is large because it contains the QR decomposition of the design matrix, which `surprisals_prob()` needs for the leverages.
So only the coefficients, fitted values and surprisal probabilities are kept, and the fitted model and the design matrix are removed.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

X <- as.matrix(dtm[reviews$id, Matrix::colSums(dtm > 0) >= 500])
fit <- lm(points ~ log(words) + X, data = reviews, model = FALSE)
fit_words <- list(
  coef = coef(fit),
  fitted = fitted(fit),
  p = surprisals_prob(fit, approximation = "gpd")
)
rm(fit, X)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-fit
#| include: false
#| dependson: [wine-dtm, wine-text-reviews]

fit_words <- local({
  X <- as.matrix(dtm[reviews$id, Matrix::colSums(dtm > 0) >= 500])
  fit <- lm(points ~ log(words) + X, data = reviews, model = FALSE)
  list(
    coef = coef(fit),
    fitted = fitted(fit),
    p = surprisals_prob(fit, approximation = "gpd")
  )
}) |>
  cache("wine_text_points")
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points-fit

reviews <- reviews |>
  mutate(fitted = fit_words$fitted, p = fit_words$p, flagged = p < 0.001)
coefs <- sort(fit_words$coef[-(1:2)])
names(coefs) <- sub("^X", "", names(coefs))
head(coefs, 10)
tail(coefs, 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points

r2_words <- cor(reviews$points, reviews$fitted)^2
top_pos <- reviews |> filter(points > fitted) |> slice_min(p, n = 6)
top_neg <- reviews |> filter(points < fitted) |> slice_min(p, n = 6)
tonnelles <- top_pos |> filter(grepl("barnyard", description))
top_great <- top_pos |> filter(points >= 96)
# The prose describes the coefficients and the largest residuals in each direction
stopifnot(
  NROW(text_features) - NROW(reviews) == 7,
  length(coefs) == 979,
  round(r2_words, 2) == 0.65,
  all(
    c("lacks", "thin", "flat", "sugary", "short", "simple") %in%
      names(head(coefs, 10))
  ),
  all(
    c("gorgeous", "beautiful", "wonderful", "opulent") %in%
      names(tail(coefs, 10))
  ),
  sum(grepl("^20[0-9][0-9]$", names(tail(coefs, 10)))) == 3,
  between(sum(reviews$flagged), 90, 110),
  sum(top_pos$points >= 96) == 5,
  NROW(tonnelles) == 1,
  tonnelles$points == 92,
  round(tonnelles$fitted) == 83,
  all(sapply(
    c(
      "powerhouse",
      "flat-out dazzling",
      "knockout",
      "almost medicinal intensity",
      "memorable",
      "^95-97"
    ),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_great$description))
  )),
  all(abs(top_great$fitted - mean(reviews$points)) < 2.5),
  !any(
    c("powerhouse", "dazzling", "knockout", "memorable", "95", "97") %in%
      names(coefs)
  ),
  all(top_neg$points <= 83),
  all(sapply(
    c(
      "asphalt",
      "Band-Aid",
      "Roquefort",
      "attention for very long",
      "brown around",
      "elegance"
    ),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_neg$description))
  )),
  !any(c("barnyard", "asphalt", "band", "roquefort") %in% names(coefs)),
  coefs["flat"] < -1,
  coefs["medicinal"] < -0.5,
  coefs["rustic"] < -0.5,
  coefs["long"] > 0.5,
  coefs["elegance"] > 0.5
)
```

The model explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * r2_words)`% of the variation in the points.
Doubling the length of a review adds `r sprintf("%.1f", log(2) * fit_words$coef[2])` points to its expected score if the extra words are all rare ones, leaving the counts of the common words unchanged.
The words with the most negative coefficients name faults, such as "lacks", "thin", "flat" and "sugary", or damn with faint praise, such as "simple" and "short".
Those with the most positive coefficients are superlatives, such as "gorgeous", "beautiful" and "wonderful", and years, which occur in advice on when to drink a wine (e.g., "Drink 2023--2035"), given mainly for wines worth keeping.

`r english::Words(sum(reviews$flagged))` reviews have surprisal probabilities below 0.001, `r english::words(sum(reviews$flagged & reviews$points > reviews$fitted))` of them with more points than predicted.
The six least probable reviews in that direction are printed below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-top
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points
#| class-output: wrap

reviews |>
  filter(points > fitted) |>
  slice_min(p, n = 6) |>
  with(paste(points, "points.", description))
```

Five of these are wines with 96--98 points, but the model predicts only `r round(min(top_great$fitted))`--`r round(max(top_great$fitted))` points for them, close to the average of `r round(mean(reviews$points))` points for all reviews.
Their reviews praise them in words too rare to be among the predictors, such as "powerhouse", "dazzling", "knockout" and "memorable", while some of their common words count against them.
"Flat-out dazzling" contains "flat", whose coefficient is `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["flat"])`, and "an almost medicinal intensity" contains "medicinal", whose coefficient is `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["medicinal"])`.
A bag of words gives a word the same weight whatever words surround it.
One review starts with "95-97.\ Barrel sample.", the taster's range of scores for a wine tasted before it was bottled.
The text states the score, but "95" and "97" are not among the predictors, so the model has to predict the points from the other words, which suggest a score close to the average.

The exception is the third, with `r tonnelles$points` points, whose review is critical: "A rustic wine, with definite barnyard flavors … the tannins and old wood tastes intrude too much."
The model predicts `r round(tonnelles$fitted)` points, and nothing in the text suggests a wine worth 92.
Perhaps the points were recorded against the wrong review; either way, this is the kind of anomaly a conditional model is meant to find.

The six least probable reviews with fewer points than predicted are printed below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-bottom
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points
#| class-output: wrap

reviews |>
  filter(points < fitted) |>
  slice_min(p, n = 6) |>
  with(paste(points, "points.", description))
```

These are wines with 80--83 points, whose reviews describe the faults in vivid words that are too rare to be among the predictors, such as "asphalt", "Band-Aid" and "Roquefort".
Others use favourable words to unfavourable effect: a wine that "won't hold your attention for very long", and "fading elegance" in a wine that is "brown around the edges".
The coefficients of "long" and "elegance" are `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["long"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["elegance"])`.

The conditional model has found two kinds of anomaly.
A few reviews, such as the third one above, really do disagree with their points.
The others printed above are reviews that a bag of words cannot read: the words that carry their meaning are too rare to be among the predictors, or a common word means something different in context, as in "flat-out dazzling" and "fading elegance".
A model of the language itself can take some of that context into account.

## Language-model surprisals {#sec-text-lm}

Language models are the engines behind chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude.
A language model estimates the probability distribution of the next token in a sequence, given all the tokens that have come before it.
A chatbot treats the user's prompt as the start of a sequence, samples the next token from this distribution, appends it to the sequence, and repeats, so that its reply is generated one token at a time.

To find anomalies, we can use the same distribution the other way round.
Instead of generating new text, we give the model text that already exists, and ask how probable each token is, given the tokens before it.
A document made up of improbable tokens has a high surprisal, and is a candidate anomaly.

Let $x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iL_i}$ denote the $L_i$ tokens of document $i$.
The probability of the whole document is the product of the probabilities of each token, given the tokens before it, so the surprisal of the document is the sum of the surprisals of its tokens:
$$
  s_i = -\log f(x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iL_i}) = \sum_{j=1}^{L_i} s_{ij},
  \qquad
  \text{where}\qquad s_{ij} = -\log f(x_{ij} \mid x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,j-1}).
$$
Each token surprisal $s_{ij}$ depends on all the tokens that come before it, which is how a language model takes context into account.
For example, "edges" is not a common word in wine reviews, but after "Looking brown around the" it is almost certain.

A document with more tokens has more to predict, so its surprisal tends to be larger.
To compare documents of different lengths, we can use the mean surprisal per token,
$$
  \bar{s}_i = \frac{s_i}{L_i} = \frac{1}{L_i} \sum_{j=1}^{L_i} s_{ij}.
$$

Suppose the model gave every token in a document a probability of $1/k$, as if it were picking each one at random from $k$ equally likely tokens.
Then every token surprisal would be $\log k$, and so would the mean.
The **perplexity** of a document reverses this: it is the number of equally likely tokens the model would have to be choosing between to be as surprised by the document as it actually is.
It equals $e^{\bar{s}_i}$, so a mean surprisal of 3 nats per token corresponds to a perplexity of about 20.

The bag of words of @sec-text-numbers is the simplest language model, in which each token is independent of the others, so that $f(x_{ij} \mid x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,j-1}) = f(x_{ij})$, and context is ignored altogether.
At the other extreme are **large language models**, which are neural networks trained to predict each token from all the tokens before it.
They are called "large" because of their size: they have billions of parameters, and are trained on trillions of tokens of text.
That size lets them use the meaning of the whole of the preceding text, so they predict the next token far better than any model based on counting words.

### Token surprisals from OLMo 2

The model used here is the smallest version of OLMo 2\ [@OLMo2025], with about a billion parameters.
Unlike most large language models, it has been published along with the data used to train it.
A model that had seen these reviews during training would find them unduly predictable, so it is useful to be able to check whether it did.
A search of the training data\ [@Liu2024] for passages from a sample of about 200 of the reviews found almost none of them.

The tokens of a large language model are not words.
The text is split into pieces from a fixed vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, so that common words are single tokens (each including the space before it), while rarer words are split into several pieces.
Each review is preceded by the prompt "Wine review:" on a line of its own, so that the model knows what kind of text follows.
Without it, the first few tokens of each review are much more surprising, because the model has no way of knowing that it is reading a wine review.

The model is run from R using the **`reticulate`** package, which calls the Python packages **`torch`** and **`transformers`**.
The first time the code is run, `py_require()` installs these packages (and Python itself if necessary), and `from_pretrained()` downloads the model, which is about 6 GB.

The function `token_surprisals()` computes the surprisal of every token in a batch of reviews.
Passing a batch through the model at once is much faster than passing the reviews one at a time, as the computations for the whole batch are done together as operations on large arrays.
However, every review in a batch must have the same number of tokens, so shorter reviews are padded to the length of the longest, and the computation on the padding is wasted.
Sorting the reviews by length, and putting 16 reviews of similar length in each batch, keeps the padding to a minimum.
The batches are kept small to limit the memory needed, as at every position of every review the model returns a score for each of the 100,000 tokens in its vocabulary.
Even with batching, computing the surprisals for all the reviews takes several hours on a desktop computer, and longer still without a graphics processing unit (GPU).

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true

library(reticulate)
py_require(c("torch", "transformers"))
torch <- import("torch")
transformers <- import("transformers")
model_name <- "allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B"
tokenizer <- transformers$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained(model_name)
olmo <- transformers$AutoModelForCausalLM$from_pretrained(model_name)

# Surprisal of each token in a batch of texts, given the prompt and the tokens before it
token_surprisals <- function(texts, prompt = "Wine review:\n") {
  input <- tokenizer(texts, return_tensors = "pt", padding = TRUE)
  # Start each text with the beginning-of-text token and the prompt
  start <- c(tokenizer$bos_token_id, unlist(tokenizer$encode(prompt)))
  m <- length(start)
  start <- torch$tensor(list(as.list(start)))$expand(length(texts), -1L)
  ids <- torch$cat(list(start, input$input_ids), dim = 1L)
  mask <- torch$cat(
    list(torch$ones_like(start), input$attention_mask),
    dim = 1L
  )
  logits <- with(torch$no_grad(), olmo(ids, attention_mask = mask)$logits)
  # Log probabilities of each token of the texts, from the position before it
  n <- ids$size(1L) - m
  log_probs <- torch$log_softmax(logits$narrow(1L, m - 1L, n), dim = -1L)
  next_ids <- ids$narrow(1L, m, n)
  surprisal <- -log_probs$gather(-1L, next_ids$unsqueeze(-1L))$squeeze(-1L)
  # Transpose so that the tokens of each text are consecutive, dropping padding
  keep <- t(mask$narrow(1L, m, n)$numpy() == 1)
  tibble(
    text = col(keep)[keep],
    token_id = as.integer(t(next_ids$numpy())[keep]),
    surprisal = t(surprisal$numpy())[keep]
  )
}

# Batches of 16 reviews of similar length, to reduce padding
by_length <- wine_reviews$id[order(nchar(wine_reviews$description))]
batches <- split(by_length, ceiling(seq_along(by_length) / 16))
wine_tokens <- lapply(batches, \(b) {
  token_surprisals(wine_reviews$description[b]) |>
    mutate(id = b[text], .before = 1)
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  select(-text) |>
  arrange(id)
# Replace the token numbers by the text of the tokens
vocab <- unique(wine_tokens$token_id)
pieces <- vapply(vocab, \(i) tokenizer$decode(list(i)), "")
wine_tokens <- wine_tokens |>
  mutate(token = pieces[match(token_id, vocab)], .after = id) |>
  select(-token_id)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-words

wine_tokens <- local({
  library(reticulate)
  py_require(c("torch", "transformers"))
  torch <- import("torch")
  transformers <- import("transformers")
  model_name <- "allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B"
  tokenizer <- transformers$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained(model_name)
  olmo <- transformers$AutoModelForCausalLM$from_pretrained(model_name)
  token_surprisals <- function(texts, prompt = "Wine review:\n") {
    input <- tokenizer(texts, return_tensors = "pt", padding = TRUE)
    start <- c(tokenizer$bos_token_id, unlist(tokenizer$encode(prompt)))
    m <- length(start)
    start <- torch$tensor(list(as.list(start)))$expand(length(texts), -1L)
    ids <- torch$cat(list(start, input$input_ids), dim = 1L)
    mask <- torch$cat(
      list(torch$ones_like(start), input$attention_mask),
      dim = 1L
    )
    logits <- with(torch$no_grad(), olmo(ids, attention_mask = mask)$logits)
    n <- ids$size(1L) - m
    log_probs <- torch$log_softmax(logits$narrow(1L, m - 1L, n), dim = -1L)
    next_ids <- ids$narrow(1L, m, n)
    surprisal <- -log_probs$gather(-1L, next_ids$unsqueeze(-1L))$squeeze(-1L)
    keep <- t(mask$narrow(1L, m, n)$numpy() == 1)
    tibble(
      text = col(keep)[keep],
      token_id = as.integer(t(next_ids$numpy())[keep]),
      surprisal = t(surprisal$numpy())[keep]
    )
  }
  by_length <- wine_reviews$id[order(nchar(wine_reviews$description))]
  batches <- split(by_length, ceiling(seq_along(by_length) / 16))
  wine_tokens <- lapply(batches, \(b) {
    token_surprisals(wine_reviews$description[b]) |>
      mutate(id = b[text], .before = 1)
  }) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    select(-text) |>
    arrange(id)
  vocab <- unique(wine_tokens$token_id)
  pieces <- vapply(vocab, \(i) tokenizer$decode(list(i)), "")
  wine_tokens |>
    mutate(token = pieces[match(token_id, vocab)], .after = id) |>
    select(-token_id)
}) |>
  cache("wine_olmo")
```

The result has one row for each token, giving its surprisal in nats (@sec-surprisals).
As tokens are discrete, a token with a surprisal of $s$ nats is given probability $e^{-s}$ by the model.
Here are the first 20 tokens of the first review.

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo-tokens
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

wine_tokens |>
  filter(id == 1) |>
  print(n = 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo-tannins
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

first_review <- wine_tokens |> filter(id == 1)
tannins <- first_review$surprisal[18:19]
# The prose describes the tokens of the first review
stopifnot(
  NROW(wine_tokens) == 6258097,
  n_distinct(wine_tokens$id) == NROW(wine_reviews),
  all(trimws(first_review$token[16:19]) == c("Firm", "t", "ann", "ins")),
  all(tannins < 0.06)
)
```

"Tannins" is split into three tokens, `" t"`, `"ann"` and `"ins"`.
Once the model has seen `" t"` after "Firm", the rest of the word is almost certain, and the surprisals of "ann" and "ins" are only `r sprintf("%.2f", tannins[1])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", tannins[2])` nats.

To score each review, its token surprisals are combined.
The code below computes the number of tokens, the mean surprisal and the perplexity of each review.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-reviews
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

lm_reviews <- wine_tokens |>
  summarise(tokens = n(), s = mean(surprisal), .by = id) |>
  mutate(perplexity = exp(s)) |>
  left_join(wine_reviews |> select(id, points, description), by = "id")
lm_reviews |>
  arrange(desc(s))
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: [wine-lm-reviews, wine-text-gmm]

lm_most <- lm_reviews |> slice_max(s, n = 12)
lm_most_reviews <- lm_most |> filter(!grepl("^Imported by", description))
lm_least <- lm_reviews |> slice_min(s, n = 6)
repeated <- lm_least |> slice_max(tokens, n = 1)
repeated_tokens <- wine_tokens |> filter(id == repeated$id)
half <- nchar(repeated$description) / 2
half_tokens <- floor(NROW(repeated_tokens) / 2)
repeated_s <- c(
  mean(head(repeated_tokens$surprisal, half_tokens)),
  mean(tail(repeated_tokens$surprisal, half_tokens))
)
by_length <- lm_reviews |>
  mutate(short = tokens <= 40) |>
  summarise(m = mean(s), sd = sd(s), .by = short)
feature_flags <- text_features$flagged[match(
  lm_most_reviews$id,
  text_features$id
)]
least_flags <- text_features$flagged[match(lm_least$id, text_features$id)]
# The prose describes the most and least surprising reviews
stopifnot(
  round(median(lm_reviews$s), 2) == 3.33,
  all(grepl("^Imported by", lm_most$description[1:3])),
  NROW(lm_most_reviews) == 9,
  all(lm_most$tokens < median(lm_reviews$tokens)),
  sum(feature_flags) == 2,
  round(cor(lm_reviews$s, lm_reviews$points), 2) == -0.06,
  by_length$m[by_length$short] > by_length$m[!by_length$short],
  by_length$sd[by_length$short] > by_length$sd[!by_length$short],
  sum(grepl("%", lm_least$description)) == 5,
  !any(least_flags),
  which(lm_least$id == repeated$id) == 4,
  substr(repeated$description, 1, half) ==
    substr(repeated$description, half + 1, 2 * half),
  round(repeated_s, 2) == c(3.31, 0.08)
)
```

### Reviews with surprising wording

@fig-wine-lm-length shows the mean surprisal of each review against its number of tokens, with the corresponding perplexity on the right-hand axis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-lm-length
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Number of tokens and mean surprisal per token (left axis) or perplexity (right axis) of the wine review descriptions, under OLMo 2.
#| fig-height: 3.5

lm_reviews |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tokens, y = s)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.01, height = 0, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      transform = exp,
      name = "Perplexity",
      breaks = c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of tokens (log scale)",
    y = "Mean surprisal (nats per token)"
  )
```

The mean surprisals of short reviews are higher and more variable than those of long reviews.
A short review has fewer tokens to average over, and less context with which to predict each of them.
The texts of the twelve most surprising reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-most
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| class-output: wrap

lm_reviews |> slice_max(s, n = 12) |> pull(description)
```

The three most surprising are import statements, which were also among the least probable descriptions in @sec-text-bow.
The other nine are genuine reviews, all of them shorter than the median review, and written in an unusual style: acids that "become jumpy", aromas that are "horsey", a wine that "convinces with simple purity" and another that feels "a bit clampy".
Only two of the nine were flagged by the text features in @sec-text-bow.
The mean surprisals are almost unrelated to the points: their correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(lm_reviews$s, lm_reviews$points))`.
So the language model finds reviews whose wording is unusual, not reviews that disagree with their points.

The six least surprising reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-least
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| class-output: wrap

lm_reviews |> slice_min(s, n = 6) |> pull(description)
```

These are the most formulaic reviews.
Five of them list the percentages of the grape varieties in a blend.
Once a review starts with "This blend of 43% Cabernet Sauvignon, 29% Merlot", the names of the other varieties are easy to predict.
None of the six were flagged by the text features in @sec-text-bow.

The fourth review is different: its text appears twice, the second copy immediately following the first.
The mean surprisal of the first half of the tokens is `r sprintf("%.2f", repeated_s[1])` nats (a perplexity of about `r round(exp(repeated_s[1]))`), close to the median for all reviews, but that of the second half is only `r sprintf("%.2f", repeated_s[2])` nats (a perplexity of `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(repeated_s[2]))`): having read the review once, the model is almost never in doubt about the next token the second time.
A bag of words cannot detect a repeated text, as repeating a document only doubles its word counts.
The repeated review is anomalous because the language model finds it highly probable, so its mean surprisal lies in the *lower* tail of the distribution, not the upper tail.
Detectors of machine-generated text are built on the same idea, as text written by a large language model is also unusually predictable under a similar model\ [@Mitchell2023; @Hans2024].

### Surprising tokens

The token surprisals also show where the surprises are within each review.
The twelve most surprising tokens are shown below, along with the tokens on either side of them.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-tokens
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

wine_tokens |>
  mutate(
    before = paste0(lag(token, 3, ""), lag(token, 2, ""), lag(token, 1, "")),
    after = paste0(lead(token, 1, ""), lead(token, 2, "")),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  slice_max(surprisal, n = 12) |>
  select(id, before, token, after, surprisal)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-tokens-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

top_tokens <- wine_tokens |> slice_max(surprisal, n = 12)
top_text <- wine_reviews$description[top_tokens$id]
# The prose describes the most surprising tokens
stopifnot(
  setequal(
    trimws(top_tokens$token),
    c(
      "aket",
      "otes",
      "RDD",
      "nis",
      "Thin",
      "fins",
      "process",
      "ini",
      "intervention",
      "negoci",
      "bowls",
      "y"
    )
  ),
  all(sapply(
    c(
      "Musaketeller",
      "tannnis",
      "finsih",
      "toprocess",
      "negociate",
      "honeysyuckle",
      "Thin Mint",
      "RDD included",
      "Case Ibidini",
      "Pinotesque",
      "interventionist",
      "bowls it right down the middle"
    ),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_text, fixed = TRUE))
  )),
  all(top_tokens$surprisal > 21)
)
```

Six of the twelve are misspellings: "Musaketeller" (for Muskateller), "tannnis", "finsih", "toprocess", "negociate" and "honeysyuckle".
The model has seen countless correctly spelt words, so the surprisal of a misspelt word is concentrated in the token where it departs from the expected spelling.
Three are names or abbreviations that the model could not have expected: "Thin Mint" (a brand of biscuit), "Case Ibidini" (a range of wines) and "RDD" (the taster's abbreviation for Ribera del Duero).
The rest are words or phrases that are unusual in a wine review: "Pinotesque", "interventionist", and a Chardonnay that "bowls it right down the middle" of popular taste.
Each of these tokens has a surprisal above 21 nats, so the model gave it a probability of less than one in a billion.

## Authorship anomalies {#sec-text-authorship}

Did Shakespeare write all of the plays attributed to him?
Which of the *Federalist* papers were written by Hamilton and which by Madison\ [@Mosteller1964]?
Was this essay written by the student who submitted it?
When the candidate authors are known, the problem is one of classification, called **authorship attribution**.
More often, there is only one candidate: the person to whom the text is credited.
Deciding whether that person wrote it, using only the texts known to be theirs, is called **authorship verification**.

Authorship verification is an anomaly detection problem\ [@Koppel2004].
The question is whether the disputed text is surprising under a model of the author's writing, fitted to their known works.
An anomalous text is unlike the author's other work, which suggests that someone else wrote it, but it does not say who.

### Style markers

The features used to describe an author's style should be the same whatever the author is writing about.
Content words are a poor choice, as they depend on the subject: a novel set at sea will use "ship" far more often than one set in a city.
Function words are better (@sec-text-numbers).
Every text uses them, so their frequencies can be estimated even from a short passage.
Writers also choose them unconsciously, so their habits are consistent from one text to the next and are difficult to imitate.
For example, in their study of the *Federalist* papers, @Mosteller1964 found that Hamilton wrote "upon" far more often than Madison, while Madison preferred "whilst" to "while".

A text is split into chunks of equal length, and each chunk $c$ is described by a $k$-vector $\bm{x}_c$ whose $j$th element, $x_{cj}$, is the number of times the chunk uses the $j$th of the $k$ most common function words.
The distance of a chunk from the author's style can then be measured by the surprisal of $\bm{x}_c$ under a probability distribution fitted to the author's chunks, so that the methods of @sec-density-methods can be used.

### Who wrote *The Royal Book of Oz*?

L. Frank Baum wrote fourteen books about the land of Oz, beginning with *The Wonderful Wizard of Oz* in 1900.
He died in 1919, but the series was too popular for his publisher to end it.
The next book, *The Royal Book of Oz* (1921), was credited to Baum and described as "enlarged and edited" by Ruth Plumly Thompson, a children's author who went on to write another eighteen Oz books under her own name.
Although it was said to be based on notes that Baum left unfinished, it is now thought to be entirely Thompson's work\ [@Binongo2003].

The `fetch_oz_books()` function returns the text of the fourteen Oz books written by Baum and fifteen of those written by Thompson, including *The Royal Book of Oz*, which is listed under her name.
Each row is a paragraph.

```{r}
#| label: oz-books-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

oz_books <- fetch_oz_books()
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-books
#| include: false

oz_books <- fetch_oz_books() |> cache("oz_books")
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-books-print
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-books

oz_books
```

The books are split into chunks of 5,000 words, dropping the incomplete chunks at the end of each book.
Each chunk is described by the number of times it uses each of 20 function words: the most common words in Baum's known books that are in the `stop_words` list of @sec-text-numbers.

```{r}
#| label: oz-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-books

oz_words <- oz_books |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  mutate(chunk = (row_number() - 1) %/% 5000 + 1, .by = title) |>
  filter(n() == 5000, .by = c(title, chunk))
baum_words <- oz_words |>
  filter(author == "L. Frank Baum", word %in% stop_words$word) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  pull(word)
baum_words
```

The counts of function words per chunk form a matrix with one row for each chunk and one column for each word.

```{r}
#| label: oz-freq
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-words

oz_freq <- oz_words |>
  filter(word %in% baum_words) |>
  count(year, title, author, chunk, word) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = word, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  select(year:chunk, all_of(baum_words))
oz_freq
```

### A model of Baum's style

Let $\bm{x}_c$ be the vector of counts of the 20 function words in chunk $c$, the $c$th row of the matrix above.
Baum's style is modelled by assuming that, for his chunks, $\bm{x}_c$ has a multivariate Normal distribution with mean $\bm{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\bm{\Sigma}$.
As the counts are relatively large, the integer nature of the data can be ignored and the numbers treated as continuous.
The surprisal of chunk $c$ under this distribution (@sec-surprisals) is
$$
  s_c = -\log f(\bm{x}_c) = \tfrac{1}{2} d_c^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \log|2\pi\bm{\Sigma}|,
$$
where $d_c$ is the Mahalanobis distance of $\bm{x}_c$ from $\bm{\mu}$ (@sec-mahal-scores).
The Mahalanobis distance takes account of the correlations between the counts of different words.
For Baum's chunks, $d_c^2$ has a $\chi^2_{20}$ distribution, so the surprisal probabilities follow directly.

Baum's books are a subset of the data believed to be free of anomalies, so $\bm{\mu}$ and $\bm{\Sigma}$ can be estimated by the mean $\bar{\bm{x}}$ and covariance matrix $\bm{S}$ of his chunks, without the robust methods of @sec-robust-cov.
But estimates from the same chunks that are being scored fit those chunks better than they would fit a new book by Baum, and the $\chi^2_{20}$ distribution no longer applies.
Leaving out one chunk at a time would not solve this, as the rest of the book shares the omitted chunk's characters, plot and narrative voice.
Instead, each of Baum's books is left out in turn, the Normal distribution is fitted to his other thirteen books, and the surprisals of the chunks of the omitted book are computed from it.
These are leave-one-out surprisals (@sec-loo-surprisals), with a whole book left out rather than a single observation.
Thompson's chunks are scored using the Normal distribution fitted to all of Baum's books.

```{r}
#| label: oz-surprisal
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-freq

X <- oz_freq |>
  select(all_of(baum_words)) |>
  as.matrix()
baum <- oz_freq$author == "L. Frank Baum"
baum_normal <- function(ref) {
  dist_multivariate_normal(list(colMeans(ref)), list(cov(ref)))
}
oz_freq$s <- surprisals(X, distribution = baum_normal(X[baum, ]))
for (book in unique(oz_freq$title[baum])) {
  this <- oz_freq$title == book
  oz_freq$s[this] <- surprisals(
    X[this, ],
    distribution = baum_normal(X[baum & !this, ])
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-chisq-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-surprisal

log_det <- determinant(2 * pi * cov(X[baum, ]))$modulus
mean_d2 <- mean(2 * (oz_freq$s[baum] - log_det / 2))
# The prose describes the mean squared Mahalanobis distance of Baum's chunks
stopifnot(round(mean_d2) == 27)
```

The squared Mahalanobis distances of Baum's chunks, computed in this way, have a mean of `r round(mean_d2)`, rather than the mean of 20 of a $\chi^2_{20}$ distribution, so the $\chi^2_{20}$ distribution would flag too many of his own chunks.
Instead, the surprisal probabilities are estimated by the rank approximation of @sec-approximate-surprisal-prob, using Baum's `r sum(baum)` leave-one-book-out surprisals as the reference sample.
That is, the surprisal probability of a chunk is estimated by the proportion of Baum's chunks with a surprisal at least as large.
There are too few of them to fit a GPD to the largest surprisals.
The table below gives, for each book, the number of chunks, their mean surprisal, and the proportion with a surprisal probability below 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: oz-prob
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-surprisal

baum_s <- oz_freq$s[baum]
oz_freq <- oz_freq |>
  mutate(p = sapply(s, \(x) mean(baum_s >= x)))
oz_summary <- oz_freq |>
  summarise(
    chunks = n(),
    s = mean(s),
    flagged = mean(p < 0.05),
    .by = c(year, title, author)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)
oz_summary |> print(n = Inf)
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-prob

baum_books <- oz_summary |> filter(author == "L. Frank Baum")
thompson_books <- oz_summary |> filter(author != "L. Frank Baum")
royal <- oz_summary |> filter(title == "The Royal Book of Oz")
royal_chunks <- oz_freq |> filter(title == "The Royal Book of Oz")
thompson_chunks <- oz_freq |>
  filter(author != "L. Frank Baum", title != "The Royal Book of Oz")
# The prose describes the surprisals of each book
stopifnot(
  NROW(oz_freq) == 230,
  sum(baum) == 116,
  identical(
    baum_words[1:8],
    c("the", "and", "to", "of", "a", "in", "i", "you")
  ),
  "said" %in% baum_words,
  between(mean(oz_freq$p[baum] < 0.05), 0.04, 0.06),
  setequal(
    baum_books$title[baum_books$flagged > 0],
    c(
      "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz",
      "The Marvelous Land of Oz",
      "Rinkitink in Oz"
    )
  ),
  all(baum_books$flagged[baum_books$year >= 1919] == 0),
  round(100 * mean(thompson_chunks$p < 0.05)) == 82,
  min(thompson_books$s) > max(baum_books$s),
  baum_books$title[which.max(baum_books$s)] == "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz",
  royal$chunks == 8,
  sum(royal_chunks$p < 0.05) == 4,
  sum(royal_chunks$s > max(baum_s)) == 2,
  sum(thompson_books$s < royal$s) == 1,
  thompson_books$title[which.min(thompson_books$s)] ==
    "The Cowardly Lion of Oz",
  cor(thompson_books$year, thompson_books$s) > 0.5,
  # The dashed line in fig-oz-surprisal separates the flagged chunks
  identical(oz_freq$p < 0.05, oz_freq$s > quantile(baum_s, 0.95, type = 1))
)
```

About 5% of Baum's chunks have surprisal probabilities below 0.05, as they must when his own chunks are the reference sample.
They come from only three books, which are also the three with the largest mean surprisals: his first two Oz books and *Rinkitink in Oz*.
None come from *The Magic of Oz* or *Glinda of Oz*, which were published after his death.
In contrast, `r round(100 * mean(thompson_chunks$p < 0.05))`% of the chunks of Thompson's other books have surprisal probabilities below 0.05.
Four of the eight chunks of *The Royal Book of Oz* have surprisal probabilities below 0.05, and two of them are more surprising than any chunk written by Baum.

The surprisal of a book is the sum of the surprisals of its chunks, if the chunks are treated as independent, just as the surprisal of a document is the sum of the surprisals of its tokens (@sec-text-lm).
So the mean surprisal of the chunks measures how surprising a book is, allowing for its length.
Every one of Thompson's books has a larger mean surprisal than every one of Baum's.
The mean surprisal of *The Royal Book of Oz* is `r sprintf("%.1f", royal$s)`, compared with at most `r sprintf("%.1f", max(baum_books$s))` (for *The Wonderful Wizard of Oz*) for Baum's books.
So the book is anomalous given Baum's known work, which is consistent with it having been written by someone else.

@fig-oz-surprisal shows the surprisal of every chunk, with the books in order of publication.
Thompson's style moved further from Baum's as she wrote more Oz books: the correlation between the year of publication and the mean surprisal of her books is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(thompson_books$year, thompson_books$s))`.
Only *The Cowardly Lion of Oz* (1923) is closer to Baum's style than *The Royal Book of Oz*.
Perhaps she imitated Baum's style more closely at first, or perhaps the notes he left did contribute something to *The Royal Book of Oz*; the function words cannot distinguish these explanations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-oz-surprisal
#| dependson: oz-prob
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Surprisals of the 5,000-word chunks of the Oz books under a Normal distribution fitted to Baum's chunks, with the books in order of publication.
#|   Each of Baum's books is left out of the fitted distribution used for its own chunks.
#|   Chunks to the right of the dashed line have surprisal probabilities below 0.05.
#| fig-height: 6

oz_freq |>
  mutate(title = reorder(title, -year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = s, y = title, colour = author)) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = quantile(baum_s, 0.95, type = 1),
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = TeX("Surprisal ($s_c$)"), y = NULL, colour = "Author")
```

### Where the differences hide

```{r}
#| label: oz-delta-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-prob

delta <- function(x, ref) {
  rowMeans(abs(scale(x, center = colMeans(ref), scale = apply(ref, 2, sd))))
}
oz_delta <- delta(X, X[baum, ])
for (book in unique(oz_freq$title[baum])) {
  this <- oz_freq$title == book
  oz_delta[this] <- delta(X[this, ], X[baum & !this, ])
}
delta_p <- sapply(oz_delta, \(d) mean(oz_delta[baum] >= d))
delta_thompson <- mean(delta_p[oz_freq$title %in% thompson_chunks$title] < 0.05)
# The prose compares Delta with the Normal surprisals
stopifnot(
  round(100 * delta_thompson) == 65,
  sum(delta_p[oz_freq$title == "The Royal Book of Oz"] < 0.05) == 4
)
```

The Normal model separates the two authors clearly, but it does not show which aspects of the word counts make Thompson's chunks surprising.
A comparison with the usual stylometric measure, **Burrows' Delta**\ [@Burrows2002], gives a clue.
Let $\bar{x}_j$ and $\hat{\sigma}_j$ be the mean and standard deviation of the $j$th count over the chunks of the author's known work.
Each count is converted to a $z$-score, $z_{cj} = (x_{cj} - \bar{x}_j)/\hat{\sigma}_j$, and Delta is the mean of their absolute values:
$$
  \Delta_c = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k |z_{cj}|.
$$
That is, $k\Delta_c$ is the Manhattan distance (@sec-distances) between $\bm{x}_c$ and the author's mean vector $\bar{\bm{x}}$, once each count has been scaled by its standard deviation.
Delta uses the same counts as the Normal model, but treats each word separately, ignoring the correlations between them.

With each of Baum's books left out in turn and the same rank approximation, Delta gives surprisal probabilities below 0.05 to `r round(100 * delta_thompson)`% of the chunks of Thompson's other books, compared with `r round(100 * mean(thompson_chunks$p < 0.05))`% for the Normal surprisals, although it also flags four of the eight chunks of *The Royal Book of Oz*.
So much of the difference between the authors lies in the correlations between the words.
The principal components (@sec-pca) of Baum's chunks show where.
The code below finds the principal components of Baum's scaled chunks, and then projects all of the chunks onto them.
Each projection is divided by the standard deviation of Baum's chunks along that component, and averaged over the chunks of Thompson's books (including *The Royal Book of Oz*).

```{r}
#| label: oz-pca
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-prob

baum_pca <- prcomp(X[baum, ], scale. = TRUE)
scores <- predict(baum_pca, X)
pc_shift <- colMeans(scores[!baum, ]) / baum_pca$sdev
pc_shift
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-pca-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-pca

# The prose describes the shift of Thompson's chunks along each component
stopifnot(
  all(abs(pc_shift[1:4]) < 1),
  which.max(abs(pc_shift)) == 19,
  abs(pc_shift[19]) > 3.5,
  abs(pc_shift[18]) > 2.5
)
```

Along the first four components, where Baum's chunks vary most, the average of Thompson's chunks is less than one standard deviation from the average of Baum's.
The largest shifts, of about `r round(abs(pc_shift[18]))` and `r round(abs(pc_shift[19]))` standard deviations, are along the 18th and 19th components, where Baum's chunks hardly vary at all.
So Thompson's chunks are anomalous because of their combinations of word rates, rather than the rate of any one word: the anomalies are hidden in the sense of @sec-hiding.
The squared Mahalanobis distance is the sum of the squared projections onto all the principal components, each divided by the variance of Baum's chunks along that component, so it gives the most weight to the directions in which Baum's chunks vary least.
Delta, which scales each word separately, gives these directions no extra weight.

An outlier map (@sec-projection-anomalies) shows the same thing.
The chunks are projected onto the first two principal components of Baum's chunks, which explain `r round(100 * sum(baum_pca$sdev[1:2]^2) / 20)`% of their variance.
The score distance of each chunk measures how far its projection is from the centre of Baum's chunks, and the orthogonal distance measures how far the chunk is from its projection.

```{r}
#| label: oz-distances
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-pca

Z <- scale(X, center = baum_pca$center, scale = baum_pca$scale)
W <- scores[, 1:2]
R <- Z - W %*% t(baum_pca$rotation[, 1:2])
oz_freq <- oz_freq |>
  mutate(
    score_distance = sqrt(rowSums(sweep(W, 2, baum_pca$sdev[1:2], "/")^2)),
    orthogonal_distance = sqrt(rowSums(R^2)),
    book = case_when(
      author == "L. Frank Baum" ~ "Baum",
      title == "The Royal Book of Oz" ~ "The Royal Book of Oz",
      .default = "Thompson (other books)"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-distances-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-distances

od_threshold <- quantile(oz_freq$orthogonal_distance[baum], 0.95)
od_share <- mean(oz_freq$orthogonal_distance[!baum] > od_threshold)
sd_medians <- oz_freq |>
  summarise(m = median(score_distance), .by = author)
# The prose describes the outlier map
stopifnot(
  round(100 * sum(baum_pca$sdev[1:2]^2) / 20) == 29,
  round(100 * od_share) == 84,
  abs(diff(sd_medians$m)) < 0.1
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-oz-outlier-map
#| dependson: oz-distances
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Outlier map of the chunks of the Oz books, using the first two principal components of Baum's chunks.
#| fig-height: 3.5

oz_freq |>
  ggplot(aes(x = score_distance, y = orthogonal_distance, colour = book)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Score distance", y = "Orthogonal distance", colour = NULL)
```

In @fig-oz-outlier-map, the score distances of Thompson's chunks are similar to those of Baum's, but most of her chunks have larger orthogonal distances: `r round(100 * od_share)`% of them exceed the 95th percentile of the orthogonal distances of Baum's chunks.
They are anomalies in the residual space, which would be missed by looking for anomalies only in the projection onto the first two principal components.
Because Baum's chunks were used to find the principal components, their distances are a little smaller than those of a new book by Baum would be, but not by enough to explain differences as large as these.

The scaled counts `Z` also show which words make *The Royal Book of Oz* unlike Baum's books.
Below are their means over its eight chunks.

```{r}
#| label: oz-royal-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: oz-distances

royal_book <- oz_freq$title == "The Royal Book of Oz"
colMeans(Z[royal_book, ]) |>
  sort() |>
  round(2)
```

```{r}
#| label: oz-royal-words-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: oz-royal-words

royal_z <- sort(colMeans(Z[royal_book, ]))
thompson_z <- colMeans(Z[!baum & !royal_book, ])
# The prose describes the mean z-scores of the Royal Book of Oz
stopifnot(
  identical(names(royal_z)[1:4], c("to", "that", "and", "but")),
  names(royal_z)[20] == "his",
  royal_z[["his"]] > 1.5,
  royal_z[["to"]] < -2,
  all(thompson_z[c("that", "but", "said", "his")] * c(-1, -1, -1, 1) > 1),
  thompson_z[["said"]] < -2.5
)
```

Thompson used "to", "that", "and" and "but" less often than Baum, and "his" more often.
Her other books share most of these differences, and also use "said" much less often than Baum's.
Some of the differences may reflect the stories rather than the writers.
Baum's books have more dialogue than Thompson's.
Her books also use "she" and "her" less often than his, which suggests that more of her central characters are male.
Function words are less affected by content than other words, but their rates still depend partly on the story being told.

## Summary {#sec-text-summary}

Each method in this chapter converts documents to numbers, and then looks for documents with small surprisal probabilities under a model of typical text.
The methods differ in how much of the text they use, from word counts with no regard to order, to every token in the context of all the tokens before it.

- **Bag-of-words anomalies**: each document is reduced to its word counts, which form a large and sparse document-term matrix.
  A few interpretable features of each document, mostly computed from its word counts, such as its length, its share of function words, the rarity of its words, its sentiment and its punctuation, can be scaled robustly and modelled with a multivariate density, so that anomalous documents are those with unusual features or unusual combinations of features.
  Features that are averages over the words of a document are noisy for short documents, which are therefore more likely to be flagged.
  When other variables are recorded with each document, a regression on the word counts gives conditional surprisals, which find documents whose wording disagrees with those variables.
  Because a bag of words ignores context, it cannot read words that are too rare to be among the predictors, or common words whose meaning depends on the words around them.
- **Language-model surprisals**: a language model gives the probability of each token given the tokens before it, so the surprisal of a document is the sum of the surprisals of its tokens.
  The mean surprisal per token (or the perplexity) allows documents of different lengths to be compared.
  The token surprisals also show where the surprises are within a document, such as misspellings and unexpected names.
  Both tails of the distribution are of interest: unusually high surprisals indicate unusual wording, while unusually low surprisals indicate formulaic or repeated text, or text generated by a similar model.
  The model should not have been trained on the documents being scored, as it would then find them unduly predictable.
- **Authorship anomalies**: authorship verification asks whether a disputed text is surprising under a model fitted to the author's known work.
  Function words make good style markers, as their rates depend less on the subject than those of content words, and writers use them unconsciously.
  The chunks of a text are not independent, so the reference sample of surprisals is obtained by leaving out a whole work at a time.
  The surprisal probabilities are then estimated by the rank approximation.
  Differences in style can hide in combinations of words, along the directions in which the author's own chunks vary least, so methods that ignore the correlations between words, or project onto the leading principal components only, can miss them.
  An anomalous text is unlike the author's other work, but the method cannot say who wrote it.
